as.e: From Middle English as, als(a), alswa, from Old English eallswā (“just so; as”), thus representing a reduced form of also.
as.g: To such an extent or degree; to the same extent or degree.

ascend.e: From Middle English ascenden, borrowed from Old French ascendre, from Latin ascendō (“to go up, climb up to”), from ad (“to”) + scandō (“to climb”); see scan. Unrelated to accede other than common ad prefix.
ascend.g: To move upward, to fly, to soar.

ascension.e: From Middle English ascencioun, from Old French ascension, from Latin ascēnsiō, ascēnsiōnem (“ascent”).
ascension.g: The act of ascending; an ascent.

ascent.e: Formed from ascend on the model of descend/descent.
ascent.g: The act of ascending; a motion upwards.

ascribe.e: From Middle English ascriben, from Old French ascrivre (“inscribe, attribute, impute”), from Latin āscrībere (“to state in writing”), equivalent to a- + scribe.
ascribe.g: To regard as arising from a specified cause or source.

ash.e: From Middle English asche, asshe, aske, from Old English acse, asċe, axe, axse, æsċe, from Proto-West Germanic *askā, from Proto-Germanic *askǭ (“ash”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs- (“to be dry; to burn; hearth; ashes”). Breton and Cornish ster (“stars”), Welsh sêr (“stars”), Latin āreō (“to be dry or parched.
ash.g: The solid remains of a fire.

ash.e: From Middle English asch, asche, assh, from Old English æsċ, from Proto-West Germanic *ask, from Proto-Germanic *askaz (“ash”), from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃s- (“ash”). The "ligature" sense is a semantic loan from Old English æsċ, whence also the synonymous doublet æsc.
ash.g: A shade tree of the genus Fraxinus.

ashamed.e: From Middle English ashamed, aschamed, from Old English āsċamod, past participle of Old English āsċamian (“to be ashamed”), equivalent to a- + shame + -ed.

ashore.e: From a- + shore; see also onshore.
ashore.g: On the land as opposed to onboard.

aside.e: From Middle English aside, asyde, a-side, oside, from Middle English on side, from Old English on sīdan (literally “on (the) side (of)”), equivalent to a- + side.
aside.g: To or on one side so as to be out of the way.

ask.e: From Middle English asken, axen, from Old English āscian, from Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eys- (“to wish; request”).
From Middle English aske, arske, ascre, from Old English āþexe (“lizard, newt”), from Proto-West Germanic *agiþahsijā (“lizard”), a compound of *agiz (“snake, lizard”) + *þahsuz (“badger”).

asked.e: From the close pronunciation to arsed in Received Pronunciation.
asked.g: Arsed (bothered; willing to make an effort).

asking.e: From Middle English askinge, askande, from Old English āsciende, from Proto-West Germanic *aiskōndī, present participle of Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn (“to ask”), equivalent to ask + -ing.
asking.g: That asks; that expresses a question or request.

asleep.e: From Middle English aslepe, equivalent to a- (“in, on”) + sleep.
asleep.g: In a state of sleep; also, broadly, resting.

asp.e: From Middle English aspe, from Old French aspe, from Latin aspis, aspidis (“asp, viper”), from Ancient Greek ἀσπίς (aspís, “shield; Egyptian cobra Naja haje”); compare Middle English aspide.
From Middle English aspe (aspen (in compounds)), from Old English æspe (æspan (in compounds)), from Proto-West Germanic *aspu, from Proto-Germanic *aspō, from Proto-Indo-European *Hosp-.

aspire.e: From Middle English aspiren, from Old French aspirer, from Latin aspīrō (“breathe on; approach; desire”).
aspire.g: To have a strong desire or ambition to achieve something.

ass.e: From Middle English asse, from Old English assa, back-formed from assen (“she-ass”), from Celtic (compare Old Irish asan, Old Cornish asen), from Latin asinus. Sense “stupid person” from the animal's reputation for stubbornness, going back to antiquity (compare Latin asinus (“slow-witted person”)).
ass.g: Any of several species of horselike animals, especially Equus asinus, the domesticated of which are used as beasts of burden.

ass.e: Variant of arse; used chiefly in North America. Ultimately from Middle English ars, ers, from Old English ærs, ears, from Proto-West Germanic *ars, from Proto-Germanic *arsaz (compare Old High German ars (German Arsch), Old Norse ars, Old Frisian ers), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁órsos (compare Ancient Greek ὄρρος (órrhos)).

assail.e: From Middle English assailen, from Old French assaillir, assalir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“at, towards”) + salīre (“jump”).
assail.g: To attack with harsh words or violent force.

assailant.e: From Old French assaillant, from the verb assaillir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“to, towards”) + salīre (“to jump”). Equivalent to assail + -ant.
assailant.g: Someone who attacks or assails another violently, or criminally.

assassinate.e: From assassin + -ate, after Middle French assassiner.
assassinate.g: To murder someone, especially an important person, by a sudden or obscure attack, especially for ideological or political reasons.

assault.e: From Middle English assaut, from Old French noun assaut, derived from the past participle of the verb assalir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“at, towards”) + salīre (“jump”). Spelling Latinized around 1530 to add an l.
assault.g: A violent onset or attack with physical means, for example blows, weapons, etc.

assay.e: From Middle English assay (noun) and assayen (verb), from Anglo-Norman assai (noun) and Anglo-Norman assaier (verb), from Old French essai.

assemble.e: From Middle English assemblen, from Old French assembler (“to assemble”), from Medieval Latin assimulāre (“to bring together”), from ad- + simulō (“copy, imitate”), from similis (“like, similar”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”).

assembly.e: From Middle English assemblee, from Anglo-Norman asemblee (Old French asemblee, French assemblée). By surface analysis, assemble + -y.
assembly.g: A set of pieces that work together in unison as a mechanism or device.

assent.e: From Middle English assent (noun) and assenten (verb), from Old French assent (noun) and assentir (verb), from Latin assentiō (whence as-).

assert.e: From Latin assertus, perfect passive participle of asserō (“declare someone free or a slave by laying hands upon him; hence free from, protect, defend; lay claim to, assert, declare”), from ad (“to”) + serō (“join, range in a row”).
assert.g: To declare with assurance or plainly and strongly; to state positively.

assess.e: From Middle English assessen, from Old French assesser, from Medieval Latin assessare, originally the frequentative of Latin assessus, past participle of assidēre, from ad (“to, towards, at”) + sedeō (“sit; settle down”).
assess.g: To determine, estimate or judge the value of; to evaluate; to estimate.

assign.e: From Middle English assignen, from Old French assigner, asigner, from Latin assignō, from ad- + signō (“mark, sign”).
assign.g: To designate or set apart (something) for some purpose.

assignment.e: From Middle English assignement, from Old French assignement. By surface analysis, assign + -ment.
assignment.g: The act of assigning; the allocation of a job or a set of tasks.

assist.e: From Middle English assisten, from Old French assister (“to assist, to attend”), from Latin assistō (“stand at, bestand”, verb).

assistance.e: From Middle English assistance, from Middle French assistance, from Medieval Latin assistentia, from Latin assistō (“to stand at”). By surface analysis, assist + -ance.
assistance.g: Aid; help; the act or result of assisting.

assistant.e: From Middle English assistent, from Middle French assistant, from assister. By surface analysis, assist + -ant.
assistant.g: Having a subordinate or auxiliary position.

associate.e: From Middle English associat(e) (used participially as well as adjectively up to Early Modern English), from Latin associātus, the perfect passive participle of associō (“to join, unite”), from ad- + sociō, from socius (“shared, common, kindred”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix).
associate.g: Joined with another or others and having lower status.

associate.e: From Middle English associat(e) (“associated, allied”) (the verb *associaten is not found in Middle English writings and only attested at a later period), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.
associate.g: To join in or form a league, union, or association.

assume.e: From Latin assūmō (“accept, take”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + sūmō (“take up, assume”).
assume.g: To authenticate by means of belief; to surmise; to suppose to be true, especially without proof.

assurance.e: From Middle English assuraunce, from Old French asseürance, from asseürer; as if assure + -ance.
assurance.g: The act of assuring; a declaration intended to inspire full confidence; something designed to give confidence to someone.

assure.e: From Old French asseurer (Modern French assurer), from Latin ad- + securus (“secure”).
assure.g: To make sure and secure; ensure.

astonied.e: Apparently from astony, astonie, from Old French estonner, from Vulgar Latin *extonare.
astonied.g: In shock or confusion; bewildered, astonished.

astonish.e: Probably an alteration (due to words ending in -ish: abolish, banish, cherish, establish, furnish, etc.) of earlier astony, astone, astun (“to astonish, stun”), from Middle English astoneyen, astonen (“to stun, astonish”), variant of stonen, stoneyen (“to stun, astonish”) prefixed with a-.

astound.e: From Middle English astouned, astoned, astuned, past participle of astounen, astonen, astunen (“to astonish”).

astray.e: From Middle English astraien or by apheresis straien, from Old French estraier (“to stray”), from late Medieval Latin extravagari (“to wander beyond”), from Latin extra (“beyond”) + vagārī (“to wander, stray”).
astray.g: Away from the proper path; in a wrong or unknown direction.

astrologer.e: From Middle English astrologer, astrologier, astrologere, formed from Middle English astrologie or Latin astrologus + Middle English -ere, equivalent to astrology + -er. Ousted imported Middle English astrologien (“astrologer”), borrowed from Old French astrologien.
astrologer.g: One who studies or practices astrology.

asunder.e: From Middle English asunder, asonder (“apart in position, distant; apart in movement; to pieces; alone, separately; distinct in kind, different”), asondri (“distinct, separate”), onsunder, onsondre (“apart, asunder; alone, separately; especially, particularly (?)”).
asunder.g: Of two or more people or things:

asunder.e: From Middle English asondren (“to alienate; to separate; to depart; to part company; to disappear”), from Old English asundran, āsundrian (“to disjoin; to separate; to sunder, put asunder; to sever”) (possibly influenced by onsundrum (adverb): see etymology 1), from ā- (prefix meaning ‘away; from’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *úd (“away.
asunder.g: To set apart (one or more people or things) from other people or things; to put asunder, to separate, to sunder.
